questions.title: What is the DOM, and why is it described as a tree structure?
questions.description:
The DOM (Document Object Model) is how the browser represents an HTML page in memory, as a tree of objects called nodes. The element is the root of the tree, and every other element (like ,
,

) is a node inside it, nested the same way the HTML was written. Each node can have child nodes, and every node except the root has exactly one parent. JavaScript uses this tree to read, change, add, or remove any part of the page, because every piece of the page -- elements, text, attributes -- is represented somewhere in this tree.
keyPoints: The DOM represents an HTML page as a tree of nodes, built by the browser from the HTML.
The <html> element is the root; every other element is nested inside it as a child or a deeper descendant.
Each node (except the root) has exactly one parent, and can have zero or more children.
JavaScript reads and changes the page by working with this tree, not with the raw HTML text.

examples.title: A small HTML tree

questions.title: How does the DOM handle whitespace in HTML, like spaces and line breaks?
questions.description: When the browser parses HTML, the spaces, tabs, and line breaks you put between tags often become real (but invisible) text nodes in the DOM tree. For example, if you put each child element on its own line with indentation, the browser creates small text nodes containing just that whitespace, sitting in between the real elements. This matters because looping over a node's children the wrong way (using childNodes instead of children) can accidentally include these invisible whitespace text nodes, which can cause confusing bugs when you expect to see only element nodes.
keyPoints: Spaces, tabs, and line breaks between HTML tags usually become real (but invisible) whitespace text nodes.
childNodes includes these whitespace text nodes; children only includes real element nodes.
Confusing childNodes with children is a common source of bugs when counting or looping over "child elements".

examples.title: childNodes vs children

questions.title: What are HTML entities, and why do you need them?
questions.description: HTML entities are special codes used to display characters that would otherwise be confused with HTML syntax, or that are hard to type directly. For example, writing a literal < or > inside text would be read as the start of a tag, so you write < and > instead, and the browser displays < and >. Entities also let you write other special characters, like & for a literal ampersand (&),   for a non-breaking space, or named entities like © for characters that are hard to type, like ©. When JavaScript reads text from the page with a property like textContent, entities are automatically turned back into their real characters.
keyPoints: Entities let you safely write characters with special meaning in HTML, like < and >, using < and >.
& writes a literal ampersand (&), and   writes a non-breaking space.
Named entities like © let you write special characters that are hard to type directly.
JavaScript's textContent (and similar properties) gives you back the real decoded characters, not the raw entity codes.

examples.title: Decoding a few common entities

questions.title: What are the different node types in the DOM, like element nodes and text nodes?
questions.description:
Every piece of an HTML page becomes a "node" in the DOM, but not all nodes are the same kind. The most common ones are element nodes (like
or

, which can have attributes and children) and text nodes (the actual text inside an element, with no tags of its own). There are a few other, rarer node types too, like comment nodes, for HTML comments. Each node has a nodeType property (a number) and a nodeName property (a short description) that tell you which kind of node it is, which is useful when you write code that walks through the DOM tree and needs to treat text differently from elements.
keyPoints:
Element nodes represent HTML tags, like
or

; they can have attributes and child nodes.
Text nodes hold the plain text inside an element, with no tags of their own.
Comment nodes represent HTML comments (<!-- ... -->).
Every node has a nodeType (a number) and a nodeName, which tell you what kind of node it is.

examples.title: The standard nodeType values

questions.title: How do you move (traverse) from one DOM node to another, like to its parent or next sibling?
questions.description: Traversing the DOM means moving from one node to a related one, using properties built into every element. parentNode (or parentElement) gets the node's parent. children gets its child elements, and firstElementChild / lastElementChild get just the first or last one. nextElementSibling and previousElementSibling move sideways, to the next or previous element at the same level. These properties let you walk through the page's structure in JavaScript, instead of searching for elements by id or class every single time.
keyPoints: parentNode / parentElement moves up to the containing element.
children, firstElementChild, and lastElementChild move down to an element's children.
nextElementSibling and previousElementSibling move sideways, between elements at the same level.
These properties only consider other elements (not whitespace text nodes), unlike their older, Node-based equivalents like nextSibling.

questions.title: What are the different ways to select (find) elements in the DOM?
questions.description: JavaScript gives you several methods to find elements on a page. getElementById("id") finds one element by its unique id. getElementsByClassName("name") and getElementsByTagName("tag") return a live collection of all matching elements. The more modern and flexible methods are querySelector("css-selector"), which returns the first matching element, and querySelectorAll("css-selector"), which returns all matching elements, using the same selector syntax you would write in CSS, like ".item", "#main", or "div > p". querySelector / querySelectorAll are usually preferred today, because CSS selectors can express much more complex conditions than the older methods.
keyPoints: getElementById finds exactly one element, by its unique id attribute.
getElementsByClassName / getElementsByTagName return a live collection of matching elements.
querySelector returns the first element matching a CSS selector; querySelectorAll returns all of them.
CSS selectors (used by querySelector / querySelectorAll) can express much more complex conditions than the older methods.

questions.title: How do you change existing DOM elements, like their text or their position in the page?
questions.description: Once you have selected an element, you can change it in several ways. textContent lets you read or replace all the text inside an element. innerHTML lets you read or replace the element's content as an HTML string, which also lets you insert new tags, but can be risky with untrusted input, since it can introduce unwanted scripts. To move elements around, methods like appendChild, insertBefore, and the newer append / prepend / before / after let you add a node at a specific position, and removeChild (or the newer remove()) takes a node out of the page.
keyPoints: textContent reads or replaces only the text inside an element (tags inside are treated as plain text).
innerHTML reads or replaces the content as HTML, so it can add real new tags, but can be unsafe with untrusted input.
appendChild / append and insertBefore / before / after add nodes at a specific position in the tree.
removeChild (or the newer element.remove()) takes a node out of the page.

examples.title: Reading and changing content

questions.title: How do you create new DOM elements with JavaScript?
questions.description: To add something new to a page, you first create the element in memory with document.createElement("tagName"), which returns a new, empty element that is not yet part of the page. You can then set its content (with textContent or innerHTML), set attributes (with setAttribute, or by setting a matching property), and finally attach it to the real page by appending it to an existing, already-visible element, using a method like appendChild or append.
keyPoints: document.createElement("div") creates a new element, but it is not visible yet -- it only exists in memory.
You can set its text/content and attributes before adding it to the page.
The element only appears on the page once you attach it, usually with appendChild or append on an existing, visible element.

questions.title: How do you read and change an element's attributes, inline styles, and CSS classes?
questions.description: getAttribute("name") and setAttribute("name", "value") let you read or change any HTML attribute, like src or href. For styling, element.style.propertyName lets you set one inline CSS style directly, for example element.style.color = "red". For working with CSS classes, classList gives you methods like add, remove, toggle, and contains, which are the recommended way to change which CSS classes are applied to an element, instead of rewriting className as one whole string.
keyPoints: getAttribute / setAttribute read or write any HTML attribute by name.
element.style.propertyName sets one inline CSS style directly, like element.style.color = "red".
classList.add / remove / toggle / contains are the recommended way to work with an element's CSS classes.
Changing classList is usually better than rewriting className, because it does not accidentally remove other classes.

questions.title: How can you control an element's position on the page and animate it with JavaScript?
questions.description: An element's size and position can be read with methods like getBoundingClientRect(), which returns its width, height, and distance from the edges of the browser window. To move an element, you usually combine CSS positioning (like position: absolute, with top/left) with JavaScript that changes those style values. For smooth animation, modern code normally relies on CSS transitions or CSS animations, triggered by changing a class or style from JavaScript, or on the Web Animations API, rather than manually updating styles in a loop, because the browser can run CSS-based animations more smoothly.
keyPoints: getBoundingClientRect() tells you an element's current size and position on the screen.
Moving an element usually means changing its CSS position properties (like top/left) from JavaScript.
Smooth animations are normally done with CSS transitions/animations, or the Web Animations API, not manual style updates in a loop.
JavaScript often just triggers the animation (for example by adding a class), while the browser's rendering engine handles the smooth motion.

examples.title: Reading position, triggering an animation

questions.title: What is the contentEditable feature, and what does it do?
questions.description: Setting the contentEditable attribute (or property) to "true" on an HTML element turns it into an editable area, directly in the browser, without needing a <textarea> or <input>. The user can click inside it and type, just like a simple text editor, and the result becomes part of the page's real HTML. This is the basic technique behind many rich text editors on the web. Because the user can type any HTML-like content, developers need to be careful about how this content is later read and used, to avoid security problems like unwanted scripts being inserted.
keyPoints: contentEditable="true" makes a normal element directly editable by the user, like a mini text editor.
It is the basic technique behind many rich text (WYSIWYG) editors.
The edited content becomes real HTML, so it must be handled carefully to avoid security issues, like unwanted scripts.

questions.title: What are the main HTML form elements, and what is each one used for?
questions.description: Forms are built from several specialized elements. <input> is the most common one, and its type attribute decides its behavior: "text" for plain text, "checkbox" for a yes/no choice, "radio" for choosing one option from a group, "password" for hidden text, and more. <textarea> is for longer, multi-line text. <select>, together with <option> children, creates a dropdown list to choose from. <button> (or an <input type="submit">) triggers an action, usually submitting the form. JavaScript can read and set the current value of any of these using their value property, or checked for checkboxes and radio buttons.
keyPoints: <input> covers many behaviors through its type attribute: text, checkbox, radio, password, and more.
<textarea> is for longer, multi-line text input.
<select> with <option> children creates a dropdown list.
<button> (or input type="submit") triggers an action, usually submitting the form.
JavaScript reads/writes an input's current value with .value (or .checked for checkboxes/radio buttons).

examples.title: Reading form input values
